questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A ball of mass 140 g is moving towards the ground at an angle of 25°. It hits the ground at 20 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ and bounces off with a speed of 15 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ at an angle of 20°.

What is the magnitude of the impulse exerted on the ball?
questions.stemText: A ball of mass 140 g is moving towards the ground at an angle of 25°. It hits the ground at 20 m s−1 and bounces off with a speed of 15 m s−1 at an angle of 20°. What is the magnitude of the impulse exerted on the ball? A 1.9 N s B 2.0 N s C 4.9 N s D 32 N s

options.label: A
options.text: 1.9 N s

options.label: B
options.text: 2.0 N s

options.label: C
options.text: 4.9 N s

options.label: D
options.text: 32 N s

questions.difficultyReason: Students must identify the angle between velocity vectors and use their vector difference to calculate impulse.
questions.misconception: Ignoring the horizontal change in momentum

explanation.body: The angle between the incoming and outgoing velocity vectors is $45^\circ$. The cosine rule gives $(\Delta v)^2=20^2+15^2-2(20)(15)\cos45^\circ$, so $\Delta v=14.2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The impulse magnitude is $\Delta p=m\Delta v=(0.140)(14.2)=2.0\ \mathrm{N\,s}$ to two significant figures.

perOption.A: Uses only the vertical change in momentum.
perOption.C: Adds the two momentum magnitudes as if the velocity reversed along a straight line.
perOption.D: Overstates the vector change, which is bounded by the sum of the initial and final momentum magnitudes of $4.9\ \mathrm{N\,s}$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
Two stationary ice-skaters Charlie and Sam, each of mass $60\ \mathrm{kg}$, are directly facing one another on an ice-skating rink. Charlie throws a $1.5\ \mathrm{kg}$ ball towards Sam with a horizontal speed of $2.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Sam catches the ball and throws it back to Charlie with the same horizontal speed.

What is the speed of Charlie after catching the ball?

A $0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
B $0.063\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
C $0.12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
D $0.13\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$

stemImage.alt: Question 5: Two stationary ice-skaters Charlie and Sam, each of mass 60 kg, are directly facing one another on an ice-skating rink. Charlie throws a 1.5 kg ball towards Sam

appearances.originalFile: grail:14529 (ACJC) 2024 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: Momentum conservation must be applied separately to the throw and catch with consistent signs.
questions.misconception: Assuming Charlie and the returning ball move in opposite directions.

explanation.body: Take rightward as positive and conserve momentum for Charlie and the ball during the throw. From $0=(1.5)(2.5)+60u$, Charlie recoils at $u=-0.0625\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. When Charlie catches the returning ball, $(60)(-0.0625)+(1.5)(-2.5)=(61.5)v$. This gives $v=-0.122\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, so Charlie's speed is $0.12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Treats the returning ball's momentum as opposite to Charlie's recoil momentum.
perOption.B: Uses Charlie's speed immediately after the throw.
perOption.D: Uses Charlie's mass alone for the final moving mass, giving a speed of $0.125\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ before rounding.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A small ball P moves with speed v towards another identical ball Q along a line joining the centres of the two balls. Ball Q is at rest initially and they collide elastically.

Which of the following shows the final velocities of the balls?
questions.stemText: A small ball P moves with speed v towards another identical ball Q along a line joining the centres of the two balls. Ball Q is at rest initially and they collide elastically. Which of the following shows the final velocities of the balls? A  B  C  D

appearances.originalFile: grail:19926 ACJC 2025 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must check both momentum and relative speed against the pictured velocities.
questions.misconception: Assuming momentum conservation alone guarantees elasticity.

explanation.body:
For balls of mass $m$, the initial momentum is $mv$, so the final momentum must also be $mv$. Options A and B give $mv$, while C gives $\tfrac12mv$ and D gives zero.

An elastic collision has equal relative speeds of approach and separation. A gives a separation speed of $v$, whereas B gives zero and fails to conserve kinetic energy.

perOption.A: Correct. Both momentum and the relative speed are conserved.
perOption.B: Conserves momentum but gives zero relative speed of separation, so kinetic energy is lost.
perOption.C: Gives a total final momentum of $\tfrac34mv-\tfrac14mv=\tfrac12mv$.
perOption.D: Gives zero total final momentum because the two momenta cancel.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The soccer ball approaches a player at velocity u = 12 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. Assume that the mass of the foot is much greater than that of the ball and that the collision is elastic.

At what velocity v should the player’s foot move in order to stop the ball upon contact?
questions.stemText: The soccer ball approaches a player at velocity u = 12 m s–1. Assume that the mass of the foot is much greater than that of the ball and that the collision is elastic. At what velocity v should the player’s foot move in order to stop the ball upon contact? A v = 12 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ in the direction opposite to the original velocity of the ball. B v = 6.0 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ in the direction opposite to the original velocity of the ball. C v = 6.0 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ in the same direction as the original velocity of the ball. D v = 0.12 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ in the same direction as the original velocity of the ball.

options.label: A
options.text: v = 12 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ in the direction opposite to the original velocity of the ball.

options.label: B
options.text: v = 6.0 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ in the direction opposite to the original velocity of the ball.

options.label: C
options.text: v = 6.0 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ in the same direction as the original velocity of the ball.

options.label: D
options.text: v = 0.12 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ in the same direction as the original velocity of the ball.

appearances.originalFile: ASRJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1 for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Needs relative speed of approach = separation with a massive moving foot.
questions.misconception: Assuming the foot must move towards the ball to stop it

explanation.body: Take the ball’s initial direction as positive and let $m$ and $M$ be the masses of the ball and foot. With the ball stopped after impact, momentum conservation gives $mu+Mv=Mv_1$, where $v_1$ is the foot’s final velocity. The elastic collision gives equal relative speeds of approach and separation, so $u-v=v_1$. Substituting gives $2Mv=(M-m)u$, so for $M\gg m$, $v\approx u/2=6.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in the ball’s original direction.

perOption.A: Reverses the direction and uses the full approach speed instead of half.
perOption.B: Reverses the direction of the required foot velocity.
perOption.D: Uses far less than half the ball’s initial speed.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Two blocks with masses of 500 g and 400 g are moving towards each other at speeds of 2.0 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ and 3.0 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ as shown.

The two blocks stick together after the collision and move off with a common speed.

What is the speed and the direction of motion of the blocks after the collision?
questions.stemText: Two blocks with masses of 500 g and 400 g are moving towards each other at speeds of 2.0 m s-1 and 3.0 m s-1 as shown. -1 -1 2.0 m s 3.0 m s 400 g 500 g The two blocks stick together after the collision and move off with a common speed. What is the speed and the direction of motion of the blocks after the collision? A 0.22 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ to the left B 0.22 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ to the right C 2.4 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ to the left D 2.4 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ to the right

options.label: A
options.text: 0.22 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ to the left

options.label: B
options.text: 0.22 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ to the right

options.label: C
options.text: 2.4 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ to the left

options.label: D
options.text: 2.4 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ to the right

appearances.originalFile: grail:16130 2022 H2 CJC Physics Promo Paper 1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: Uses opposite signs for the initial velocities in one momentum equation.

explanation.body: Take right as positive. Conservation of momentum gives $(0.5)(2.0)+(0.4)(-3.0)=(0.5+0.4)v$. Thus $v=-0.22\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, so the blocks move left.

perOption.A: Correct. The combined velocity is negative with right taken as positive.
perOption.B: Reverses the direction of the net initial momentum.
perOption.C: Adds the magnitudes of opposing momenta and assigns the result to the left.
perOption.D: Adds the magnitudes of opposing momenta and assigns the result to the right.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A tennis ball of mass 60 g is dropped vertically from a height. It hits the ground with a speed of 21 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ downwards and then bounces upwards with an initial speed of 14 m $\mathrm{s}^{-}$ $^{1}$. The time of contact between the ball and the ground is 0.30 s.

What is the magnitude of the impulse provided by the ground?
questions.stemText: A tennis ball of mass 60 g is dropped vertically from a height. It hits the ground with a speed of 21 m s-1 downwards and then bounces upwards with an initial speed of 14 m s- 1. The time of contact between the ball and the ground is 0.30 s. What is the magnitude of the impulse provided by the ground? A 0.42 N s B 2.1 N s C 7.0 N s D 2100 N s

appearances.originalFile: grail:16130 2022 H2 CJC Physics Promo Paper 1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: Tracks a velocity reversal and distinguishes net impulse from contact impulse.
questions.misconception: Confusing net impulse with contact impulse

explanation.body: The key takes the impulse to be the ball's change in momentum. With upward positive, $m(v_f-v_i)=0.060[14-(-21)]=2.1\ \mathrm{N\,s}$.

perOption.A: Subtracts the speed magnitudes despite the reversal in direction.
perOption.B: Correct. It gives the net impulse used by the key.
perOption.C: Divides the momentum change by contact time, giving the mean net force in newtons.
perOption.D: Uses 60 as the mass in kilograms instead of converting 60 g to 0.060 kg.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A moving object P approaches head-on a stationary object Q with velocity v, as shown.

The two objects collide elastically.

After collision Q moves to the right with speed 0.4 v.

What is the speed of P after the collision?
questions.stemText: A moving object P approaches head-on a stationary object Q with velocity v, as shown. Q P v The two objects collide elastically. After collision Q moves to the right with speed 0.4 v. What is the speed of P after the collision? A 0 B 0.4 v C 0.6 v D v
questions.difficultyReason: Direct use of relative speed of approach equals relative speed of separation.
questions.misconception: Assuming the masses are equal, or that P must stop or keep going forward

explanation.body: Take right as positive and let $V$ be P's final velocity. In an elastic collision, the relative speed of approach equals the relative speed of separation, so $v-0=0.4v-V$. Thus $V=-0.6v$ and P's speed is $0.6v$.

perOption.A: Stopping P would leave a separation speed of only $0.4v$.
perOption.B: Even if P rebounds at $0.4v$, the separation speed would be only $0.8v$.
perOption.D: If P rebounded at $v$, the separation speed would be $1.4v$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The diagram below shows two spheres undergoing a head-on elastic collision. Sphere X has mass 2M while sphere Y has mass M. Both are moving with speed v towards each other.

Which of the following statements is incorrect?
questions.stemText: The diagram below shows two spheres undergoing a head-on elastic collision. Sphere X has mass 2M while sphere Y has mass M. Both are moving with speed v towards each other. v v Y X M 2M Which of the following statements is incorrect? A The two spheres cannot come to rest at the same time. B The total kinetic energy of both spheres is conserved throughout the collision. C The magnitude of the change in momentum for each sphere is the same after the collision. D The force exerted by sphere X on Y is equal and opposite to the force exerted by Y on X during the collision.

options.label: A
options.text: The two spheres cannot come to rest at the same time.

options.label: B
options.text: The total kinetic energy of both spheres is conserved throughout the collision.

options.label: C
options.text: The magnitude of the change in momentum for each sphere is the same after the collision.

options.label: D
options.text: The force exerted by sphere X on Y is equal and opposite to the force exerted by Y on X during the collision.

appearances.originalFile: MI Physics/H2/2026 PU3 H2 PHYSICS PRELIM P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Distinguishing kinetic energy conservation overall from what happens during the contact.
questions.misconception: Believing kinetic energy is conserved at every instant during an elastic collision

explanation.body: An elastic collision has the same total kinetic energy before and after impact. During contact, some kinetic energy can temporarily become elastic potential energy as the spheres deform. The claim that kinetic energy is conserved throughout the collision is therefore the incorrect statement.

perOption.A: This statement is true because the conserved total momentum is $2Mv-Mv=Mv$, so the spheres cannot both be at rest.
perOption.B: Correct. Kinetic energy can temporarily become elastic potential energy.
perOption.C: This statement is true because conservation of momentum requires equal and opposite momentum changes.
perOption.D: This statement is true by Newton’s third law.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: Body X of mass 2.5 kg undergoes a head-on collision with body Y of mass 1.0 kg. X and Y have initial speeds of $6.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and $4.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ respectively, moving towards each other. [Diagram: X moving right at $6.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, Y moving left at $4.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.] The bodies are in contact for 20 ms. After the collision, X continues in the same direction with speed $2.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. What is the magnitude of the average force exerted on Y during the collision? A 10 N B 200 N C 250 N D 500 N

stemImage.alt: Question 9: Body X of mass 2.5 kg undergoes a head-on collision with body Y of mass 1.0 kg. Bodies X and Y have initial speeds of 6.0 m s−1 and 4.0 m s−1 respectively. The

questions.difficultyReason: Uses Newton's third law to get the force on Y from X's momentum change.
questions.misconception: Using the speed change of Y without knowing its final velocity, or ignoring direction

explanation.body: Taking X’s initial direction as positive, X changes momentum by $\Delta p_X=(2.5)(2.0-6.0)=-10.0\ \mathrm{N\,s}$. Newton’s third law gives Y the opposite impulse, $+10.0\ \mathrm{N\,s}$. The average force on Y has magnitude $F_{\mathrm{avg}}=10.0/(20\times10^{-3})=500\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Uses the impulse without dividing by the contact time.
perOption.B: Uses Y’s mass with X’s change in velocity.
perOption.C: Uses X’s final momentum of $5.0\ \mathrm{N\,s}$ in place of the $10.0\ \mathrm{N\,s}$ momentum change.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Two blocks of masses m and 2m approach each other with speeds u and 0.5u and collide head-on. A light spring of force constant k is attached to the block of mass 2m.

What is the maximum compression experienced by the spring during the collision?
questions.stemText: Two blocks of masses m and 2m approach each other with speeds u and 0.5u and collide head-on. A light spring of force constant k is attached to the block of mass 2m. What is the maximum compression experienced by the spring during the collision? A mu 2 6 k B 2 mu 2 3 k C 3 mu 2 2 k D 3mu 2 k

appearances.originalFile: RI/H2/2026 RI H2Phy Prelims P1 Questions.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Students must identify the common velocity at maximum compression and combine momentum with energy conservation.
questions.misconception: Not realising that the blocks share a common velocity at maximum compression

explanation.body:
At maximum compression the blocks move with a common velocity $v$. By conservation of momentum (taking right as positive):

$mu - 2m(0.5u) = 3mv \Rightarrow v = 0$

So all the initial kinetic energy is stored in the spring:

$\tfrac{1}{2}mu^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}(2m)(0.5u)^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$, with $v = 0$

$\tfrac{3}{4}mu^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2 \Rightarrow x = \sqrt{\dfrac{3mu^2}{2k}}$

perOption.A: Treats both velocities as being in the same direction, which gives a non-zero common velocity and too little energy stored.
perOption.B: Does not equate all of the initial kinetic energy, $\tfrac{3}{4}mu^2$, to the elastic potential energy $\tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$.
perOption.C: Correct. The common velocity is zero, so all the KE is stored as elastic PE.
perOption.D: Drops the factor $\tfrac{1}{2}$ in the kinetic energy terms, which doubles the energy stored.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A tennis ball of mass $0.060\ \mathrm{kg}$ is travelling horizontally at $12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ towards a tennis racket. The racket hits the ball and causes it to travel in the opposite direction at $18\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

The ball is in contact with the racket for $0.015\ \mathrm{s}$.

What is the average force exerted by the racket on the ball?

A. $24\ \mathrm{N}$
B. $72\ \mathrm{N}$
C. $120\ \mathrm{N}$
D. $200\ \mathrm{N}$

stemImage.alt: Question 4: A tennis ball of mass 0.060 kg is travelling horizontally at 12 m s−1 towards a tennis racket. The racket hits the ball and causes it to travel in the opposite

questions.difficultyReason: Requires opposite velocity signs in a direct impulse calculation.

explanation.body: Take the rebound direction as positive. Using $mv_f-mv_i=F\Delta t$ gives $(0.060)[18-(-12)]=F(0.015)$, so the average force is $120\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Subtracts the two speeds as if the ball kept moving in the same direction.
perOption.B: Assumes the ball starts from rest and counts only the final momentum.
perOption.D: Overestimates the force by using too large a momentum change or too short a contact time.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A ball falls vertically from a great height and rebounds from a horizontal floor. The collision with the floor lasts for a very short time.

When determining the change in momentum of the ball during the collision, its weight is often neglected.

Which statement best explains why this is a valid approximation?
questions.stemText: A ball falls vertically from a great height and rebounds from a horizontal floor. The collision with the floor lasts for a very short time. When determining the change in momentum of the ball during the collision, its weight is often neglected. Which statement best explains why this is a valid approximation? A The weight of the ball does not act while the ball is in contact with the floor. B The weight of the ball is much smaller than its momentum immediately before the collision. C The weight of the ball is balanced by the contact force from the floor during the collision. D The impulse due to the weight of the ball during the collision is much smaller than the impulse due to the contact force from the floor.

options.label: A
options.text: The weight of the ball does not act while the ball is in contact with the floor.

options.label: B
options.text: The weight of the ball is much smaller than its momentum immediately before the collision.

options.label: C
options.text: The weight of the ball is balanced by the contact force from the floor during the collision.

options.label: D
options.text: The impulse due to the weight of the ball during the collision is much smaller than the impulse due to the contact force from the floor.

questions.difficultyReason: Requires comparing the impulses delivered by gravity and the floor over the short contact time.
questions.misconception: Assuming gravity stops acting during contact

explanation.body: The ball's weight acts throughout the collision, while the floor's much greater contact force reverses the ball's momentum. Over the short contact time, the impulse due to weight is much smaller than the impulse due to the floor, so weight can be neglected when finding the momentum change.

perOption.A: The ball's weight continues to act throughout the collision.
perOption.B: Weight is a force and momentum is $mv$, so their magnitudes cannot be compared directly.
perOption.C: The floor's contact force exceeds the weight and produces the upward momentum change.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
Two trolleys P and Q of masses $2m$ and $m$ respectively move along the same straight line and collide. The total kinetic energy of the two trolleys is unchanged by the collision.

Before the collision, P moves to the right at $5.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and Q moves to the left at $4.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

What is the velocity of P after the collision?

A. $1.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ to the left
B. $1.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ to the right
C. $8.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ to the left
D. $8.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ to the right

stemImage.alt: Question 9: Two trolleys P and Q of masses 2m and m respectively move along the same straight line and collide. The total kinetic energy of the two trolleys is unchanged by

questions.difficultyReason: Requires solving simultaneous signed momentum and relative-speed equations.
questions.misconception: Assigning the other trolley's velocity to P

explanation.body: Taking right as positive, momentum conservation gives $2m(5.0)+m(-4.0)=2mv_P+mv_Q$. Since the collision is elastic, relative speed of approach equals relative speed of separation, so $5.0-(-4.0)=v_Q-v_P$. Solving gives $v_P=-1.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and $v_Q=8.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, so P moves left at $1.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.B: Interprets P's negative velocity as motion to the right.
perOption.C: Uses Q's speed and gives it the wrong direction.
perOption.D: Reports Q's velocity instead of P's.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A snooker ball of mass $m$ travels at a speed $v$ towards the side of a snooker table as shown below. The ball strikes the side of the table at an angle of $30^\circ$ to the normal and moves off with the same speed at an angle of $30^\circ$. The time of contact between the ball and the side is $\Delta t$. What is the expression for the average force acting on the ball?

[Top view. The side of the pool table is horizontal. The ball approaches from the upper right and rebounds towards the upper left, with each velocity arrow labelled $v$ and each path making $30^\circ$ with the dashed normal at the point of impact.]

A $\frac{mv}{\Delta t}$
B $\frac{mv\cos30^\circ}{\Delta t}$
C $\frac{2mv\cos30^\circ}{\Delta t}$
D $\frac{2mv\sin30^\circ}{\Delta t}$

stemImage.alt: Question 11: A snooker ball of mass m travels at a speed v towards the side of a snooker table as shown below. The ball strikes the side of the table at an angle of 30° to t

appearances.originalFile: TJC/H2 Physics/2026 H2 Prelim Paper 1 final.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: It requires resolving momentum perpendicular to the cushion and accounting for its reversal.
questions.misconception: Ignoring the sign reversal of the normal momentum

explanation.body: The momentum component parallel to the side of the table is unchanged, so the average force is perpendicular to the side. Taking away from the side as positive, the average force is $\Delta p/\Delta t=[m(v\cos30^\circ)-m(-v\cos30^\circ)]/\Delta t=2mv\cos30^\circ/\Delta t$.

perOption.A: Uses the initial momentum magnitude in place of the change in normal momentum.
perOption.B: Uses just one normal component and misses the reversal.
perOption.D: Doubles the component along the side, which is the component that stays constant.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: A neutron moving with an initial velocity u has a head-on elastic collision with a stationary proton. After the collision, the velocity of the neutron is v and that of the proton is w. Taking the masses of the neutron and proton to be equal, which one of the following statements is wrong?
questions.stemText: A neutron moving with an initial velocity u has a head-on elastic collision with a stationary proton. After the collision, the velocity of the neutron is v and that of the proton is w. Taking the masses of the neutron and proton to be equal, which one of the following statements is wrong? A Conservation of momentum shows that u = v + w. B Conservation of energy shows that $u^{2}$ = $v^{2}$ + $w^{2}$. C The fact that the collision is elastic implies that the neutron and proton move off in opposite directions with equal speeds. D The momentum and energy equations taken together imply that the speed of the proton after the collision is the same as that of the neutron before the collision.

options.label: A
options.text: Conservation of momentum shows that u = v + w.

options.label: B
options.text: Conservation of energy shows that $u^{2}$ = $v^{2}$ + $w^{2}$.

options.label: C
options.text: The fact that the collision is elastic implies that the neutron and proton move off in opposite directions with equal speeds.

options.label: D
options.text: The momentum and energy equations taken together imply that the speed of the proton after the collision is the same as that of the neutron before the collision.

appearances.originalFile: TJC/H2 Physics/2026 H2 Prelim Paper 1 final.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: It requires applying both momentum and kinetic-energy conservation to interpret the result of a collision between equal masses.
questions.misconception: Equating an elastic collision with equal and opposite outgoing velocities

explanation.body: Conservation of momentum gives $u=v+w$, and conservation of kinetic energy gives $u^2=v^2+w^2$. Squaring the first equation and comparing with the second gives $2vw=0$. For an actual collision the proton takes the incoming velocity, $w=u$, and the neutron stops, $v=0$. Opposite outgoing velocities of equal magnitude would give zero total momentum, so statement C is wrong.

perOption.A: This statement correctly applies momentum conservation after cancelling the equal masses.
perOption.B: This statement correctly applies kinetic-energy conservation for an elastic collision.
perOption.C: Correct. The statement would give zero final momentum.
perOption.D: This statement correctly describes the transfer of velocity to the initially stationary proton.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A ball X moving on a frictionless table with kinetic energy $E$ and momentum $p$ makes a head-on inelastic collision with an identical ball Y which is initially at rest. Which of the following options shows possible values for the total kinetic energy and total momentum of both X and Y after the collision?
[Table columns are total kinetic energy and total momentum.]
A $E/2$, $p/2$
B $E/2$, $p$
C $E$, $p/2$
D $E$, $p$

stemImage.alt: Question 7: A ball X moving on a frictionless table with kinetic energy E and momentum p makes a head-on inelastic collision with an identical ball Y which is initially at

questions.difficultyReason: It requires distinguishing conservation of momentum from loss of kinetic energy.
questions.misconception: Assuming momentum is lost in an inelastic collision

explanation.body: The inelastic collision reduces the total kinetic energy, so $E/2$ is the only listed energy that can apply. Since Y starts at rest, the initial total momentum is $p$, and conservation of momentum keeps the total at $p$ after the collision.

perOption.C: Keeps the kinetic energy unchanged and incorrectly halves the momentum.
perOption.D: Keeps the kinetic energy unchanged despite the inelastic collision.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The diagram shows two spherical masses approaching each other head-on at an equal speed u. One has mass 2m and the other has mass m.

Which diagram represents the situation after an elastic collision?
questions.stemText: The diagram shows two spherical masses approaching each other head-on at an equal speed u. One has mass 2m and the other has mass m. m 2m u u Which diagram represents the situation after an elastic collision? A 2m m B 2m m C 2m m D 2m m
questions.difficultyReason: The student can identify the correct diagram by comparing the signed velocities.

explanation.body: In an elastic collision, the relative speed of separation equals the relative speed of approach. The two masses approach at a relative speed of $2u$, and only C gives that separation speed.

perOption.A: The masses move in the same direction and separate at $2u/3-u/6=u/2$.
perOption.D: The masses move together, so their separation speed is zero.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
Particles X (of mass 4 units) and Y (of mass 9 units) move directly towards each other, collide and then separate. If $\Delta v_X$ is the change of velocity of X and $\Delta v_Y$ is the change in velocity of Y, what is the magnitude of the ratio $\frac{\Delta v_X}{\Delta v_Y}$?

A $\frac{9}{4}$
B $\frac{3}{2}$
C $1$
D $\frac{2}{3}$

questions.difficultyReason: Requires matching momentum-change magnitudes and solving for the speed-change ratio.
questions.misconception: Confusing equal impulses with equal velocity changes.

explanation.body: By Newton's third law, the particles exert equal and opposite forces on each other during the collision, so their momentum changes are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. Hence $4|\Delta v_X|=9|\Delta v_Y|$, giving $\left|\frac{\Delta v_X}{\Delta v_Y}\right|=\frac{9}{4}$.

perOption.B: Takes a square root as if the momentum change depended on velocity squared.
perOption.C: Equates velocity changes despite the different masses.
perOption.D: Uses an inverted square-root mass ratio instead of the inverse mass ratio.
